title: Chapter 59 — Squid
paragraphs: Slowly wading through the meadows of brit, the Pequod still held her course northeast toward the island of Java. A gentle breeze pushed her keel, so that in the surrounding calm her three tall tapering masts swayed mildly to the lazy wind, like three palm trees on a plain. And still, at wide intervals in the silvery night, the lonely, beckoning jet would be seen.

But one transparent blue morning, when a stillness almost supernatural spread over the sea — though with no stagnant calm about it — when the long burnished path of sunlight on the waters seemed a golden finger laid across them, commanding some secrecy, when the slippered waves whispered together as they softly ran on — in this profound hush of the visible world, a strange apparition was seen by Daggoo from the main-masthead.

In the distance, a great white mass lazily rose, and rising higher and higher, disentangling itself from the blue, at last gleamed before our bow like a snow-slide, freshly slipped from the hills. Thus glistening for a moment, it slowly sank. Then once more it arose and silently gleamed. It did not seem a whale — and yet, was this Moby Dick? thought Daggoo. Again the phantom went down, but reappearing once more, with a stiletto-like cry that startled every man from his drowse, the negro yelled out, "There! There again! There she breaches! Right ahead! The White Whale, the White Whale!"

At this the seamen rushed out to the yardarms, the way bees rush to the branches at swarming time. Ahab stood bareheaded on the bowsprit in the sweltering sun, one hand thrust far behind him, ready to signal his orders to the helmsman, and turned his eager gaze in the direction that Daggoo's outstretched, motionless arm was pointing from aloft.

Perhaps the drifting company of that one still, solitary jet had slowly worked on Ahab, so that he was now ready to link ideas of mildness and calm with the first sight of the particular whale he was hunting; or perhaps his eagerness got the better of him. Whichever it was, the moment he clearly made out the white mass, he gave orders, with quick intensity, to lower the boats.

The four boats were soon in the water, Ahab's in the lead, all pulling hard toward their prey. Soon the thing went down, and as we waited, oars raised, for it to reappear — look! — it slowly rose again in the very spot where it had sunk. Almost forgetting Moby Dick for the moment, we now stared at the most astonishing phenomenon the secret seas have yet revealed to mankind. A vast pulpy mass, furlongs long and wide, of a gleaming cream color, lay floating on the water, with countless long arms radiating from its center, curling and twisting like a nest of anacondas, as though groping blindly for any unlucky object within reach. It had no face or front that could be made out, no conceivable sign of either feeling or instinct; it simply rippled there on the waves, an unearthly, shapeless, chance-like apparition of life.

As with a low sucking sound it slowly disappeared again, Starbuck, still gazing at the agitated waters where it had sunk, exclaimed with a wild voice — "I would almost rather have seen Moby Dick and fought him than have seen you, white ghost!"
"The great live squid, which, they say, few whale-ships have ever seen and returned to their ports to tell of it."
But Ahab said nothing. Turning his boat, he sailed back to the vessel. The rest silently followed.

Whatever superstitions sperm whalemen in general have attached to the sight of this object, one thing is certain: because a glimpse of it is so very rare, that fact alone has done much to give it an air of ill omen. It is seen so seldom that, although every one of them declares it the largest living thing in the ocean, very few have more than the haziest notions of its real nature and shape. Even so, they believe it provides the sperm whale with his only food. Other kinds of whales find their food above water, where men can watch them eating; but the spermaceti whale gets all his food in unknown zones below the surface, and what exactly it consists of can only be worked out by inference. Sometimes, when hard pressed, he will throw up what are thought to be the detached arms of the squid, some of them more than twenty, even thirty, feet long. The whalemen imagine that the monster these arms belonged to usually clings by them to the ocean floor, and that the sperm whale, unlike other species, has teeth so that he can attack it and tear it apart.

There seems some ground for imagining that the great Kraken of Bishop Pontoppodan may ultimately turn out to be a squid. The way the Bishop describes it — as alternately rising and sinking, with certain other details he provides — in all this, the two correspond. But much allowance must be made for the incredible size he assigns it.

By some naturalists who have vaguely heard rumors of the mysterious creature spoken of here, it is classed among the cuttlefish, to which, indeed, in certain outward respects it would seem to belong — but only as the Anak of the tribe — its biblical giant.
